newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU barley exports up sharply in past month.
newsitem.headline: EU barley exports up sharply in past month.

text.p: European Union barley exports actually sold or in the pipeline have more than tripled in the past month, figures suppied to member countries show.

The EU authorised 1.684 million tonnes of commercial barley exports between July 1 and October 8, almost twice the comparable level for last year, according to a breakdown given to the EU's cereals management committee on October 10 and supplied to Reuters. The September 10 figure was 477,000 tonnes.
On October 10 the committee granted licences to export a further 185,786 tonnes of barley, mainly from the open domestic market rather than EU-controlled intervention storage.
EU officials have said the Commission is switching towards a policy of favouring the open market over intervention. The latter is dominated by German supplies and is nearly sold out.
France, Denmark and Britain -- with little or nothing in intervention -- will be the main beneficiaries, they said.
"We cannot base our whole policy on intervention. We don't have enough quantities and nor would it be reasonable," a Commission official said last week.
Less than 200,000 tonnes of German, Danish or Swedish barley remain for export after recent active sales from Germany.

The EU is gradually supplying licences to cover the sale of 1.4 million tonnes of optional-origin barley to Saudi Arabia by the end of the year. Around half of the amount is tipped to come from the EU, with 500,000 tonnes of that from the open market.

However, latest awards from both the free market and intervention valued European barley at $138 per tonne, fob, which is still at the high end of the range of export prices traders need to balance their books for Saudi Arabia.
Barring any surge in domestic prices, EU officials have said they intend to cover the Saudi business, implying some increase in barley export refunds from the current 31 Ecus per tonne.
But officials say the EU also remains concerned about the impact of higher barley refunds on malt.
The Commission is locked in a dispute with malt exporters over the level of their refunds, which are usually 30 percent above the barley refund and tend to go up in step with barley.
The Commission last week delivered a rebuff to maltsters by refusing to raise their refund from the current 32.5 Ecus. The maltsters want the refund lifted to at least 40 Ecus.
Export sources said the European Commission considered European malt to be cheap after an abundant crop and did not consider the refund worth adjusting.
They also said maltsters had taken up ample export licences at the current fixed rate, or 10 percent of their annual needs of two million tonnes.
Malt industry groups and the Commission declined to comment.
The EU export breakdown dated October 8 showed that 185,000 tonnes of licences were in circulation by that day, compared with 8,000 tonnes at the same point last year.
